content: In 2018, two training of trainers sessions were conducted in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces, involving doctors and female health visitors. These sessions utilized an adapted clinical handbook to address adolescent sexual abuse. Plans are underway to extend this training to the district level. Punjab province is also developing a monitoring and evaluation component to assess improvements in the knowledge, attitudes, and skills of healthcare providers. Meanwhile, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province is preparing to conduct a facility readiness evaluation to identify necessary changes at the service delivery level. The adoption of guidelines will be evaluated by measuring changes in provider knowledge, attitudes, and skills in responding to violence. Traditional cultural practices often reflect the values and beliefs of a community, some of which are beneficial, some neutral, and others harmful, particularly to women. Harmful traditional practices include female genital mutilation (FGM), child marriage, female infanticide, menstrual stigma, and discriminatory nutritional practices. FGM involves the partial or total removal of external female genitalia or other injuries to female genital organs for non-medical reasons. Child marriage refers to formal or informal unions before the age of 18. Harmful traditional practices among adolescents are a significant global issue. Over 200 million girls and women are estimated to live with the effects of FGM, which is predominantly performed on girls under 18. FGM is most prevalent in 30 countries in Africa, as well as in some countries in Asia and the Middle East. In countries like Djibouti, Guinea, Mali, Somalia, and Sudan, the prevalence of FGM exceeds 75% among women and girls aged 15–49. However, an adolescent girl today is about one-third less likely to undergo FGM compared to 30 years ago. Each year, approximately 12 million girls are married before the age of 18, with girls being five times more likely than boys to marry before the age of 15. In 25 high-prevalence countries, about 36% of women aged 18–22 were married before 18. Globally, the proportion of women married as children has decreased by 15% in the past decade. FGM has no known health benefits and can cause immediate complications such as hemorrhage, shock, infections, and even death. Long-term consequences include post-traumatic stress disorder, menstrual problems, and pain during intercourse. Women with type III FGM are more likely to experience difficult labor and obstetric hemorrhage. Additionally, children of mothers who have undergone FGM face increased risks of stillbirth and neonatal complications. Child marriage is a leading cause of early childbirth, with 90% of adolescent births globally occurring within marriage. Adolescent pregnancies are associated with negative health outcomes, particularly among girls aged 10–14. Women married before 18 are also at higher risk of intimate partner violence and have lower educational attainment, which negatively impacts their children’s education. Prevention of harmful traditional practices requires long-term, multi-level interventions. Effective strategies include community mobilization, female empowerment, legislation against FGM, prevention counseling, education on health risks, training of healthcare workers, and promotion of alternative rites. Economic interventions, such as cash transfers or reducing school-associated costs, can also help delay marriage when combined with efforts to build individual confidence and social networks. Laws alone are insufficient to prevent child marriage; they must be complemented by programmatic efforts to empower adolescents, promote gender equity, and support girls’ education. Globally, 27 of the 30 countries where FGM is prevalent have laws banning the practice, yet it continues. There is evidence that healthcare providers are increasingly performing FGM, highlighting the need for stronger enforcement of laws and policies. Similarly, 99 countries have laws allowing girls to marry before 18 with parental consent, and exceptions under customary or religious laws often undermine legal protections. Regional model laws, such as the Southern African Development Community Parliamentary Forum Model Law, should be adopted and enforced. Legislative changes must be accompanied by efforts to address the root causes of harmful practices, build capacity at all levels, and provide protective measures for victims. Healthcare providers should be informed about the types of FGM and associated health risks to contribute to prevention efforts. Medicalization of FGM is unacceptable as it violates medical ethics and perpetuates the practice. Adolescents who have undergone FGM or child marriage often lack access to care and support, and many delay seeking care due to embarrassment or shame. Stakeholders at all levels must work together to prevent FGM and child marriage, ensuring that adolescents and communities are informed about the consequences and available services. The WHO has issued guidelines for managing health complications from FGM, including recommendations for deinfibulation to treat urological complications and cognitive behavioral therapy for mental health issues. Guidelines for preventing early pregnancy and poor reproductive outcomes among adolescents emphasize reducing child marriage, increasing contraceptive use, and improving access to skilled care. Interventions should target political leaders, communities, and individuals to delay marriage and empower girls through education and awareness. Efforts to prevent FGM and child marriage require political will, funding, improved legislative frameworks, and community interventions to address social norms. These efforts should be complemented by increasing education and employment opportunities for adolescent girls. Healthcare providers must reject the medicalization of FGM and advocate for its prevention. Comprehensive, multi-sectoral approaches are essential to eliminate these harmful practices and protect the rights and health of adolescents.
